title: What Enterprise Buyers Actually Ask about AI Video Tools
summary: A guide to enterprise AI video evaluations, including security, compliance, branding, localization, enterprise video management, and procurement.
body_markdown:
AI video trials usually run for about a week, and by the end of it the team knows whether the tool works for them or not. Then the tool goes into a review phase where security sends a questionnaire, an AI committee asks which models touch your content, legal redlines the data processing agreement, and procurement wants to know whose budget it comes out of.


That second stage takes anywhere from a week to three months, and across the enterprise sales calls we reviewed this year it was the most common blocker, ahead of price. This guide covers the questions IT, security, AI governance, legal, and procurement teams ask about AI video tools, what a good answer looks like, and what to send them on the first day of the pilot so the review runs alongside it instead of after it.


## What do enterprise buyers ask about AI video tools during security review and procurement?


An AI video tool security review is the vendor assessment an enterprise runs before employees can put company content into a new tool. It checks certifications, where data is stored and processed, whether content trains AI models, who can access what, and the contract terms that govern all of it. It usually runs in parallel with legal and procurement.


Five groups do the asking, and each one can stop the purchase on its own. This table maps who asks what and how hard each gate is.


Who asks


What they ask


How it gates the deal


IT and security


SOC 2 Type II report, ISO/IEC 27001 certificate, pen test, security questionnaire, SSO, browser extension permissions


Hard gate. No report, no approval.


Privacy and legal


DPA, data residency, retention and deletion, sub-processors, MSA terms


Hard gate, especially for EU personal data


AI governance committee


Model training on your content, which model providers are used, voice cloning and avatar consent, human approval


Hard gate where a committee exists, and it often meets on its own schedule


Procurement and finance


Pricing model, overage terms, budget owner, pilot terms


Usually a delay rather than a stop


Content teams (L&D, education, marketing, enablement)


LMS tracking, updates, brand control, localization


Decides which tool wins the evaluation


The rest of this guide takes those questions in the order they tend to arrive.


## How long does security review and procurement take for an AI video tool?


Expect anything from one week to three months. Enterprise buyers we spoke with this year described the whole range. One security team expected to finish about a week after the vendor's documents arrived. Another buyer agreed to compress its vendor assessment to four weeks by running legal and security in parallel. A training team at a large consumer platform put procurement at anywhere from two or three weeks to two or three months, because nobody could say in advance which reviews would apply.


Usually, two things stretch the timeline.


- The first is an AI review. A public-sector software company told us its route ran through legal, an AI committee, and the executive team, with at least six weeks expected, and a healthcare company needed an architecture review to answer its AI committee's concerns after the cyber review had already passed.
- The second is budget. At one large technology company, legal wouldn't start on the contract until the purchase had at least verbal spending approval, because the tool hadn't been in the start-of-year plan.


The fix is to stop running these reviews one after another. Ask the vendor for the full security package before IT's first call, then submit to security, the AI committee, and legal in the same week. Two enterprise teams we worked with this year weren't allowed to put any company material into a new tool until a contract was signed, so their pilots ran on generic workflows and sandbox accounts. That kept the evaluation moving while the paperwork caught up.

## Which security certifications should an enterprise AI video vendor have?


At minimum, a SOC 2 Type II report and an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate. A SOC 2 Type I report describes a vendor's controls at a single point in time, while a Type II report covers how they operated over an audit period, which is why security teams ask for Type II. ISO/IEC 27001 certifies the vendor's information security management system.


Ask for the documents rather than trusting a badge on a pricing page. Check that the SOC 2 audit period is recent and that the ISO certificate's scope covers the product you're buying, not only a parent company. Most security teams will also send their own questionnaire, often the SIG, and ask for a penetration test summary.


Regulated sectors add more. If recordings could show patient data, ask directly whether the vendor will sign a HIPAA business associate agreement. Public-sector buyers may need FedRAMP. Neither follows from a SOC 2 report, so don't assume either one.


> Clueso is audited annually by independent auditors against SOC 2 Type II and ISO/IEC 27001, and its[data processing agreement](https://www.clueso.io/legal/dpa) commits to sharing a summary copy of the current report on written request.


## Is our content used to train AI models?


Get the answer in the contract, not on a website FAQ. Then ask the follow-up most buyers skip: what the vendor's AI providers do with your content. An AI video tool sends your recordings and transcripts to transcription, language model, text-to-speech, and image providers. A vendor that trains nothing can still pass your content to a provider that keeps it.


Four questions cover it. Does the vendor train any models of its own? Do its AI sub-processors confirm in writing that they won't train on your content? How long do those providers keep inputs after a request finishes? And does the vendor log model inputs and outputs for monitoring, and if so, with whom?

Its[sub-processor list](https://www.clueso.io/legal/subprocessors) also names the provider that records some model inputs and outputs for quality monitoring.

## Where is customer data stored and processed?


Treat the storage region and the processing location as two separate questions, because the answers often differ. A vendor can store your content in Frankfurt and still send it to a US-based language model when it writes a script. For EU and UK personal data, that transfer needs a legal basis, usually the EU Standard Contractual Clauses.


Ask which region holds your content at rest, which providers process it and where they're based, and how the vendor tells you when that list changes. A published sub-processor list with an advance-notice period gives your privacy team something to monitor, rather than a one-time answer that goes stale.


> Clueso stores customer content in one of three AWS regions: Mumbai, Frankfurt, or California. Its AI sub-processors are US services covered by Standard Contractual Clauses, and the[sub-processor list](https://www.clueso.io/legal/subprocessors) names each provider and its location, with changes posted 10 business days before they take effect.


## What happens to our recordings after deletion or cancellation?


Ask how long deleted content stays recoverable and how soon after cancellation everything is gone. Then ask whether the vendor will certify the deletion in writing, which your auditors may want later. Screen recordings need tighter terms than most SaaS data, because they show internal systems and often whatever customer record happened to be open at the time.

## What do IT teams check on SSO, access control, and the browser extension?


IT's first request is single sign-on through SAML, so people sign in with the company identity provider and lose access the day they leave. Role separation comes next, and it matters more for video than people expect. Subject-matter experts and compliance reviewers need to comment on a video without being able to edit or publish it.


Browser extensions get their own review, and that one can hold up a trial. A software company's pilot was paused for a couple of weeks while its IT committee approved access, so ask IT to review the extension before the trial starts rather than on the first day. Encryption is usually a quick check: ask for encryption at rest and in transit, and for the TLS version.


> On Clueso's Enterprise plan, you get SAML single sign-on and reviewer seats for people who comment without editing, and roles and permissions start on the Business plan. The[screen recorder](https://www.clueso.io/features/screen-recorder) browser extension stays dormant and collects nothing when it isn't recording, and content is encrypted at rest (AES-256) and in transit (TLS 1.2 or higher).


## How do you keep personal data out of recordings during a pilot?


Training and product videos show real software, and real software shows customer names and account numbers. A healthcare training team we spoke with flagged that its systems hold Social Security numbers and home addresses, which put security and legal review on the critical path before anyone could record.


Start with the environment. Record in a sandbox or test account filled with approved fake data, so there's nothing sensitive on screen in the first place. Then add a safety net for what slips through: blur fields while recording, and run an automatic pass that finds the emails and account IDs you missed. Our guide to[building an enterprise video production workflow](https://www.clueso.io/blog/enterprise-video-production-workflow) covers the recording side in more detail.

## What do AI governance committees ask about models, voices, and avatars?


AI committees review how a tool uses AI, separately from whether it's secure. Their questions fall into two groups.


The first group is about models. Which providers does the tool use for each job, such as transcription, scripting, voice, and images? Can you restrict it to the providers your company has approved? How will you hear about a new model or provider before it touches your content? And does the tool edit material your team created, or generate content from scratch? Some companies send AI-assisted editing and fully generated content down different approval routes, so ask which one each feature falls under.


The second group covers deepfake and consent risk, and for video it's the one that matters most. Ask how the vendor confirms that a person agreed to have their voice cloned, who can use that cloned voice once it exists, and what happens to it when the person leaves. Ask whether avatars use stock presenters or a real person's likeness, and whether your policy requires telling viewers that a voice or presenter is synthetic. Then check that a named person can approve each video before it's published.

## What do legal and procurement need before signing?


Legal starts with the data processing agreement. Check four terms: how fast the vendor must tell you about a security incident, how long after termination your data is deleted, how much notice you get before a new sub-processor is added, and whether you can object to one. For EU and UK personal data, confirm the Standard Contractual Clauses are included. Then settle whose paper the master services agreement is on, because a redline cycle on an unfamiliar MSA can outlast the security review.


Procurement cares about how the bill grows. AI video tools price per seat, per hour of exported video, per AI credit, or on some mix of these. Map the pricing model to your expected volume for the next year, and ask what happens when you go over. If the tool wasn't in this year's budget, find the budget owner before the pilot ends, because that approval can gate the legal review.

## What do L&D, education, and marketing teams check before security gets involved?


Before any of the reviews above, the teams who'll use the tool decide whether it's worth reviewing at all. Each team has at least one requirement that can rule a tool out.


Team


Requirement that can rule a tool out


What to test in the pilot


Learning & development


LMS completion tracking rather than an embedded video


Export a SCORM or xAPI package and check that completion reaches the LMS


Customer education


Updating a video when the product changes, without re-recording it


Change one screen and time the fix

Sales enablement

Customer success and support


Localization for global customers


Translate one video and have a native speaker review it

## Which security and legal answers stop an enterprise AI video deal?


Some answers end an evaluation outright, while others only push it into the next quarter. Sort them early, because the first kind needs documents in front of reviewers in week one.


These stop deals:


- Any ambiguity about whether your content trains AI models, at the vendor or at its providers.
- A missing SOC 2 Type II report or ISO/IEC 27001 certificate, or a scope that doesn't cover the product.
- A DPA your legal team can't accept, especially on deletion and sub-processor changes.
- An AI committee rejection over model providers, voice cloning, or avatars.
- No tracked LMS export when the training is mandatory.


These slow deals down:


- Browser extension approval and IT access for trial users.
- SSO setup before a wider rollout.
- Budget that wasn't planned for this year.
- Questionnaire turnaround on either side.


Get the documents to security, legal, and the AI committee in week one, and start the pilot in a sandbox so your team keeps testing while access and budget approvals catch up.


## Frequently asked questions


### How should an enterprise evaluate deepfake and consent risk when choosing an AI video tool?


Look at the two features that can imitate a real person: voice cloning and avatars. For each, ask how the vendor records consent, who in your workspace can use a cloned voice or custom likeness, how it's removed when the person leaves, and whether your policy requires disclosing synthetic voices to viewers. Then confirm a person can approve every video before it's published. In Clueso,[voice cloning](https://www.clueso.io/features/voice-cloning) is on the Enterprise plan and requires the consent of the person whose voice is cloned. The default video shows your real product on screen with an[AI voiceover](https://www.clueso.io/features/ai-voiceovers) , and[AI avatars](https://www.clueso.io/features/ai-avatars) are an optional feature you choose per video.


### What compliance standards should I look for when choosing an AI video tool for enterprise use?


Start with SOC 2 Type II and ISO/IEC 27001, plus GDPR terms in a DPA if you handle EU personal data. Add sector requirements, like HIPAA for patient data, only after confirming the vendor supports them, because neither follows from SOC 2. Clueso is SOC 2 Type II audited and ISO/IEC 27001 certified on every plan, lists GDPR on every plan, and its[DPA](https://www.clueso.io/legal/dpa) includes the EU Standard Contractual Clauses and 72-hour incident notice.


### Which AI video platform is safest for confidential internal content?


The safest choice is the one whose contract, not its marketing, rules out training on your content, names every provider that processes it, and deletes it on a fixed timeline. Pair that with your own controls: record in a sandbox with fake data and blur what's left. Clueso doesn't train on customer content and requires the same of its AI providers in writing ([privacy policy](https://www.clueso.io/legal/privacy) ), publishes its[sub-processor list](https://www.clueso.io/legal/subprocessors) , and offers blur on every plan, with automatic detection through[Magic Blur](https://www.clueso.io/features/auto-blur) on the Enterprise plan or as an add-on.


### Which AI video platforms offer EU or GDPR-compliant data residency?


Check two things separately: where content is stored at rest and where AI processing happens. Many tools store data in the EU but process it with US-based model providers, which is lawful under the Standard Contractual Clauses but should be stated in the DPA. Clueso can store customer content in Frankfurt, names its US-based AI sub-processors on its[sub-processor list](https://www.clueso.io/legal/subprocessors) , and covers those transfers with Standard Contractual Clauses in its[DPA](https://www.clueso.io/legal/dpa) .


### What should I expect to pay for an enterprise-grade AI video tool, and what's usually included?


Enterprise plans are usually custom-priced, and the main variables are seats, export hours, AI credits, and support level. What moves a plan from team to enterprise is mostly governance: SSO, reviewer roles, a security review, SLAs, and a dedicated contact.
